statement: Substance over form in international transactions (ITCA art. 3) recharacterises a roundabout transaction through a third party, including one that obtains treaty benefits indirectly, by its economic substance. The library holds the Act (kr.itca, art. 3(3)-(4), since 2026-11-10) and the Enforcement Decree, but no parameter for the ratio or the amounts, so the rule is a deny of Korean treaty caps on the predicate gaar (does the arrangement unjustly reduce the tax burden), with the parameter kr.anti_abuse.substance_over_form_principle. The general substance-over-form rule of the Framework Act on National Taxes (art. 14) is not in the library.

statement: The national withholding rate on a Korean-source dividend paid to a foreign corporation (CIT art. 98(1)(ii)) or a non-resident individual (ITA art. 156(1)(ii)) is 20%. Where a treaty's covered taxes include local income tax, those articles compare the treaty rate with the rate including the local tax, so the cap is the combined ceiling, which is how the cap stage applies it after the surtax. For a treaty whose covered taxes exclude local income tax (art. 98-7(1)(i)) the cap would limit the national tax only and the local tax would come on top; that case is not distinguished (the treaty texts' covered-tax articles are not read by the rules).

statement: ITA s8(1) makes a company resident in Malaysia for a basis year when, at any time during that year, the management and control of its business (s8(1)(b)) or, for a company not carrying on a business, of its affairs by its directors or other controlling authority (s8(1)(c)) is exercised in Malaysia. Both limbs are read through managed_in = 'my'. 'At any time during that basis year' is a lower bar than a place of effective management for the whole year, so managed_in is my whenever management and control was exercised in Malaysia during the year. Incorporation in Malaysia alone does not make a company resident.

statement: Malaysia charges no tax on a dividend paid to a company: the paying company may not deduct tax from a dividend (s108(1)) and Sch 6 para 12B(1) exempts a dividend paid to any person other than an individual where the payer is not entitled to deduct tax. The source rule reads the s108(1) parameter, which is the condition of para 12B(1) and has no start date in the library. The domestic exemption in the final slot reads the para 12B(1) parameter, in force from YA2025 because the Finance Act 2024 narrowed para 12B to persons other than individuals; for dates before 2025 that rule does not apply, although the single-tier exemption existed then in its earlier wording, which the library does not hold.

statement: From YA2025 an individual's dividends deemed derived from Malaysia (paid by a resident company, s14) are charged under s6(1)(r) and Schedule 1 Part XXII at 2% on the chargeable income in respect of the dividends in excess of RM100,000 for the year; dividends of RM100,000 or less are exempt under Sch 6 para 12B(2). The rule layer has no deduction effect: the final rule applies 2% to the gross dividend, and the exemption takes the whole dividend out when the year's total (annual_dividends_local_ccy) is at most RM100,000. Above the threshold the 2% is an upper bound: HASiL deducts RM100,000 from the dividend statutory income (Form BE 2025 notes, Mr. Razif), and P.U.(A)148/2025 r2 allocates chargeable income by A/B x C when there is other income, so the charge is at most 2% of (total - 100,000). The same charge applies to non-resident individuals (r2(2)); the source cell applies it in the same way (my.outbound_wht.dividend_tax_rate.individual, the same 2%), with the same RM100,000 exemption and the treaty exemptions. A dividend from a company not resident in Malaysia is not deemed derived from Malaysia, so Part XXII does not reach it: a resident individual's foreign dividend received in Malaysia and not exempt is chargeable income at the Schedule 1 Part I para 1 rates (my.final.progressive_bracket_n); the bracket uppers are the running sums of the table's 'first' and 'next' amounts, and the schedule is stacked on the individual's other chargeable income without the reliefs and rebates of the Act.

statement: P.U.(A)235/2022 para 4 as amended by P.U.(A)157/2024 (from 1 January 2024): a resident company, and a resident individual for dividends in relation to a partnership business in Malaysia, is exempt on foreign dividends received in Malaysia if either (a) the dividend was subjected to a tax of a similar character where it arises and that territory's highest rate is at least 15%, or (b) it employs an adequate number of employees and incurs an adequate amount of operating expenditure in Malaysia. (a) is read as payer_income_taxed (HASiL guideline para 5.2.1.4(a) accepts income tax or withholding tax on the dividend, or underlying tax on the profits it is paid from) and payer_tax_rate as the source territory's headline corporate rate; the guideline's deemed cases (no tax because of unabsorbed losses or allowances, capital gains, incentives with substance, consolidation) are not modelled, so for such profits the exemption may be missed. (b) is the predicate substance, to be answered for Malaysia (substance@my), with the factors of guideline para 5.2.1.4(c) (employees, full or part time, premises). 'Incorporated or registered under the Companies Act 2016' is not tested separately: a resident company carrying on business in Malaysia is registered under it. For 2022 and 2023 the original para 4(2) applies: both conditions of the participation route together, with no substance alternative; the English text of that paragraph is left out of the clause table by superseded.csv, so its 15% is cited from the Malay text (para 4(2)(b), 'tidak kurang daripada lima belas peratus'), and para 4(3) deems the subject-to-tax condition met under the HASiL guideline, read the same way as above. Not modelled: the Labuan category (d) added by P.U.(A)157/2024, and any exemption after 2026 (the library holds no extension for companies).

statement: Foreign income other than partnership income received in Malaysia by a resident individual is exempt from 1 January 2022 to 31 December 2026 (P.U.(A)234/2022), extended to 31 December 2036 by P.U.(A)451/2024, provided it has been subjected to tax in the country of origin. The condition is read as payer_income_taxed: the guideline (para 5.2.2.2) accepts income tax or withholding tax on the dividend, or underlying tax on the profits it is paid from; the deemed cases where no tax was imposed (losses, capital gains, incentives, consolidation) are not modelled. P.U.(A)234/2022 itself is not in the library; the 2022-2026 rule cites the enabling power (ITA s127(3)(b)) and the HASiL guideline from which the library's parameter is taken.

statement: Foreign tax on a dividend received in Malaysia is credited as bilateral credit (s132, Schedule 7) where a double taxation arrangement is in force, which is the case for all ten other jurisdictions of the library, and otherwise as unilateral credit (s133), which may not exceed half of the foreign tax (Sch 7 para 14); the credit effect cannot express that limit. Three treaties extend the Malaysian credit to the payer's tax on the profits a dividend is paid from, for a Malaysian company holding enough of the payer's voting shares: MY-SG art. 23(1) (10%), MY-TH art. 23(2) and AE-MY art. 23(2) (15%); these are the credit_underlying rules of those flows, with holding_pct read as the share of the voting shares. The other Malaysian treaties of the library give no underlying credit.
quote: The unilateral credit allowed in respect of any foreign income for a year of assessment shall not exceed half the foreign tax payable on that income for that year.

statement: Several treaties exempt dividends paid by a Malaysian company to a resident of the partner from 'any tax in Malaysia which is chargeable on dividends in addition to the tax chargeable in respect of the income of the company' (CN-MY art. 10(3), MY-VN art. 10(3), AE-MY art. 10(3), ID-MY art. 10(3), KR-MY art. 10(3), MY-TH art. 10(2)(b)). The Schedule 1 Part XXII tax charged on individuals from YA2025 is read as such an additional tax: it falls on the shareholder's dividend on top of the company's income tax. The exemption therefore takes an individual's Malaysian dividend tax to zero for a resident of the partner who is the beneficial owner (KR-MY: who is subject to Korean tax on the dividend). The other reading, that the clauses only address the former imputation system, draws on their second sentence about the adjustment of tax deducted from dividends, but the first sentence is general. KR-MY protocol para 3 asks for consultation if Malaysia introduces a further tax on dividends; that is not modelled. The rules start at each agreement's Malaysian effective date, long before the tax itself.

MY-SG art. 10(3) is drafted the same way ('where either or both of he Contracting States impose' such a tax, the art. 10(2) rates apply), so the 10% cap of MY-SG art. 10(2)(b) applies to an individual from 2025-01-01 as well, also above the 2% rate.

statement: Each of Viet Nam's ten treaties in the library obliges Viet Nam to credit (or deduct) the partner's tax on income that the treaty lets the partner tax, up to the Vietnamese tax on that income. Written as credit in vn|all|inbound|<partner>, for a company on top of the domestic art. 3(4) credit and for an individual as the only credit (D-vn-6); the procedure is art. 62(3) of the consolidated Circular. The underlying credit that hk-vn art. 22(3) and sg-vn art. 24(2)(a) give a Vietnamese company holding at least 10% of the payer is credit_underlying in vn|company|inbound|hk and |sg (thresholds hk-vn / sg-vn.inbound.indirect_credit_holding_pct_min, added in round 2). Both clauses count a direct or indirect holding; the rule reads holding_pct, the direct holding, so an indirect holder is not given the credit (conservative). Neither clause nor the Circular says whether the dividend is grossed up by the underlying tax before the Vietnamese tax is computed, so no vn.inbound.underlying_gross_up parameter is written and the optimizer credits the underlying tax against the tax on the dividend as received. Not modelled: the tax-sparing and deemed-paid clauses (cn-vn art. 23(3), id-vn art. 23(4), my-vn art. 24(3) and (6), sg-vn art. 24(2)(b), th-vn art. 23(2)(b)), which the effect vocabulary cannot express. Treaty start dates are not set on these rules: the Vietnamese inclusion rules they serve begin in 2025 (companies) and 2026 (individuals), after every treaty took effect.

statement: Date the principal purposes test applies in Viet Nam to taxes withheld at source: the first day of the calendar year after the later of the two parties' MLI entries into force (MLI art. 35(1)(a)). Viet Nam's MLI entered into force on 2023-09-01 (treaty.csv, hk-vn row), later than China's, Japan's, Singapore's and Thailand's, so the test applies from 2024-01-01 for cn-vn, jp-vn, sg-vn and th-vn (the sg-vn Annex A states only Singapore's dates; Viet Nam's is inferred the same way). For hk-vn Hong Kong reserved art. 35(7); the library's treaty row computes 2025-01-01 for Viet Nam from Hong Kong's notification received on 2024-02-22, and that date is used. Round 2: my-vn from 2024-01-01 (both parties list the agreement, Malaysia's MLI in force 2021-06-01, Viet Nam's 2023-09-01, intl.oecd.mli.parties.20260915.en); kr-vn from 2022-01-01 under the 2019 Protocol's own main-purpose test (new art. 28(1), effective for taxes withheld at source from the 1 January after its entry into force on 2021-01-20); its control test (art. 28(3)) concerns entities controlled by non-residents and is not written, since Viet Nam caps only individuals' dividends. No PPT rule for ae-vn, id-vn and in-vn: Viet Nam lists all three as covered agreements, but the partners' MLI positions are not in the library and the registered id-vn text (published by the DGT as modified by the MLI) contains no MLI provision.

statement: sg-vn art. 10(2): 5% where the beneficial owner has contributed more than 50% of the capital or more than US$10 million, 7% between 25% and 50%, 12.5% otherwise. holding_pct carries the share of capital contributed (strictly more than 50% for the 5% rate, sg-vn.outbound_wht.holding_pct_min). The US$10 million alternative is a text parameter (sg-vn.outbound_wht.holding_amount_min) and is not written as a condition. The treaty does not limit the 5% and 7% rates to companies, so the three caps are written for individuals; all are at or above the 5% Vietnamese rate on a non-resident individual's dividends, so none lowers the tax.

statement: Dividends are income under s10(1)(d), charged when they accrue in or are derived from Singapore or are received in Singapore from outside Singapore (s10(1)); a resident individual's chargeable income is taxed at Part A of the Second Schedule (s42(1)), Table 3 from the year of assessment 2024. The one-tier exemption (s13, dividends of a Singapore resident company) and the exemption of an individual's foreign-sourced income received in Singapore (s13(7A)) normally leave nothing to tax; the charge and the schedule matter when an exemption is denied, as the GAAR reading sg.anti_abuse.gaar does (deny cap:* and exempt:*). An individual's foreign dividend after a denied s13(7A) exemption is charged only when received in Singapore (s10(1)), so in the GAAR branch the remittance becomes a planning move. The figure is the tax if the Comptroller only denies the exemption: s33(2) lets the Comptroller make the adjustment the Comptroller considers appropriate, and the surcharge of s33A is not included. The dividend is stacked on the individual's other chargeable income (other_taxable_income).

statement: Singapore's credit under the UAE treaty takes into account the UAE tax on the profits of the company paying the dividend, with no holding threshold (art. 23(3)). Only the payer's own tax is meant, so the rule applies when the payer is the company whose profits bore the tax (tiers = 1, the payer itself); a UAE company paying on dividends it received (UAE-exempt) gives no credit. It matters only where the s13(8) exemption fails, that is for UAE payers taxed below the 15% of s13(9)(b). The other Singapore treaties' underlying credits are not written: every other partner in the library taxes at 15% or more, so the exemption takes the dividend out first. The unilateral credit for underlying tax (s50A(2), 25% holding) reaches only tax the payer paid in its own territory; for the only partner without a treaty, Hong Kong, a holding company's dividend income bears none, so it changes no figure and is not written.
quote: the credit shall take into account U.A.E. tax payable on the profits of the company paying the dividend
